I have been rewriting emails for senior people for about twelve years, and the first thing I do with almost every one of them is the same. I delete the opening paragraph. Not because it is badly written, but because it is almost never the beginning. The real first sentence is usually the second one, and everything before it is the writer clearing his throat in public. I hope this finds you well. I wanted to reach out. Following up on our conversation of last week. None of that is information, and the reader has seen all three before breakfast. Now, the word people always give me back is short. They tell me they will make it shorter, and that is not what I asked for. Short is about how many words there are. Concise is about how many of them are doing work. I have read four-line emails that were wordy, because three of the lines said nothing, and I have read a full page that was concise, because every paragraph carried something the reader needed to decide. So here is the test I use, and it is the only editing rule I would give anybody who writes in a second language. Take one line out. Then ask what the reader would miss. If the honest answer is nothing, the line does not go back in. Do that four or five times and you will find the strange thing: the email gets shorter and it also gets warmer, because what is left is all about the person reading it.

Quick note for the team, and I am recording it because I keep saying it one person at a time. Here is what actually happens with your emails. I read them on my phone, standing in the kitchen, before six, before anybody in this building is awake. That is my inbox hour. I make a decision about each message in a few seconds, and there are only three of them: answer now, keep it for later, or archive it. And I want you to know exactly what sends a message to archive. It is not bad grammar. I do not care about your grammar, half of this company writes in a second language and some of the clearest writing I get comes from people who learned English at thirty. What sends it to archive is this: two lines have gone by and I still do not know what you want from me. If I have to read to the bottom of a message to find the question, I will not do it at ten to six, and I will not come back to it at eleven either, because by then there are sixty more. Second thing, and this one is a favor to yourselves. Ask me one thing. When there are two questions in a message I answer the easy one, every time, and I promise you I am not doing it on purpose. And the last one. When something has gone wrong, write it with a person in it. There was a communication gap tells me nothing and it makes me suspicious. We missed it and here is what we changed tells me who I am talking to, and that email gets an answer before I put the phone down.

First I write the subject line, because it forces me to know what the message is really about. Then I open with something the other person said, so it reads as a continuation. After that I put the bottom line in one sentence, before any evidence. Then I add two short lines of proof, and I delete anything the reader would not miss. And I close with one question and a sign-off, and I send it the same day.
